query: For high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles intended for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, corrosion-related uses, and other applications requiring thermal stability, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their premelting and melting behavior and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing factor, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Surface segregation controls the premelting and melting behavior of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles; specifically, if surface segregation is inhibited by passivation, then the onset of premelting will be delayed relative to unmodified particles.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with intrinsic atomic-scale disorder both at the surface and in the bulk.
generation.intervention: Selective surface passivation treatment designed to inhibit surface segregation without altering the interior (bulk) composition.
generation.conditions: Heating experiments under controlled atmosphere using a consistent thermal ramp, spanning from sub-melting temperatures (onset of surface premelting) to complete melting, and using nanoparticles in the size range below 100 nm.
generation.structural_mediator: Modification of surface atomic arrangements by preventing segregation of low-cohesive energy clusters at the nanoparticle surface.
generation.mechanism: By passivating the surface, the formation of energetically favorable atomic arrangements that serve as nucleation sites for premelting is suppressed, thereby increasing the thermal activation barrier for surface melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: Passivated nanoparticles will exhibit a higher onset temperature for premelting and a delayed melting transition compared to unmodified (baseline) nanoparticles.
generation.baseline: Unmodified high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with natural surface segregation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for nanoparticles within typical catalytic and energy-related applications under controlled heating regimes; it may not apply to significantly larger particles or systems with different surface chemistries.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative shift in melting temperature and whether the effect is consistent across all high-entropy compositions remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles: one set modified by a surface passivation treatment to inhibit segregation, and an unmodified control set. Subject both sets to a controlled heating protocol using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) under identical atmospheric conditions. Compare the onsets of premelting and the melting profiles between the two sets.
measurements: DSC thermograms to determine temperature onsets for premelting and peak melting temperatures
Structural characterization (e.g., TEM) before and after heating to confirm retention of bulk composition and changes at the surface
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the passivated nanoparticles do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in the premelting onset temperature (or show an equivalent or lower onset temperature) compared to the unmodified control under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that surface segregation governs the melting behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways. In this article, an EFA descriptor has been developed for the purpose of capturing synthesizability of high-entropy materials. The framework has been applied to refractory metal carbides, leading to the prediction and subsequent experimental discovery of homogeneous high-entropy single phases. The method is able to quantitatively predict the relative propensity of each composition to form a homogeneous single phase, thus identifying the most promising candidates for experimental synthesis. In particular, the experiments validate the prediction that the composition MoNbTaVWC5 should have a very high propensity to form a homogeneous single phase, despite incorporating both Mo2C and W2C, which have different structures (hexagonal and/or orthorhombic instead of rock-salt) and stoichiometric ratios from the five-metal high-entropy material. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that disorder enhances the mechanical properties of these materials: HfNbTaTiZrC5 and HfTaTiWZrC5 are measured to have hardness of 32 GPa (almost 50% higher than the ROM prediction) and 33 GPa, respectively, suggesting a new avenue for designing super-hard materials. Indeed, in many phase diagrams, multiphase fields usually shrink with temperature as solid solution and melt ranges increase. However, that is not always the case. For example, the liquidus loop in the Os-Re system at 3100 °C is as wide as in Cu-Ni system at 1300 °C and shows 20 at.% difference in composition between solid and liquid phases. The narrow two-phase fields for high temperature phase transformations and melting are peculiar to intra-rare earth systems. frame.system: High‐entropy alloy nanoparticles in their as‐synthesized, compositionally complex state, intended for catalytic, sensing, energy storage, and corrosion applications where thermal stability is critical.
frame.goal: To elucidate a single testable mechanistic explanation for the control of premelting and melting behavior in these nanoparticles under high-temperature conditions.
frame.limitation: There is an incomplete understanding of how the intrinsic atomic-scale disorder, compositional heterogeneity, and surface versus bulk effects determine the onset of premelting and the subsequent melting behavior.

frame.regime: Thermal regime spanning the onset of surface premelting (sub-melting temperatures) through to complete melting, under controlled heating rates typical in thermal analysis experiments.
prior_attempts: Empirical measurements and simulations have correlated overall cohesive energies with melting points, yet these studies did not isolate the contribution of nanoscale compositional disorder versus surface segregation effects.
Prior approaches investigated melting behavior based on average bulk properties, failing to provide a controlled comparison that distinguishes between surface-initiated versus bulk melting phenomena.
